Can a squatter take ownership of a Maryland house?

Only after meeting every element of adverse possession for 20 years, and a court has to agree. A person who simply moves into a vacant house has no ownership claim the day they arrive.

The 20 year number comes from Courts and Judicial Proceedings 5-103(a). It gives a person 20 years from the date the cause of action accrues either to file suit to recover possession of land or to enter the land. After that window the true owner's right to recover is cut off. The statute leaves the common-law doctrine of prescription alone for rights such as easements, and it preserves the limits in Real Property 6-103 and 8-107.

Years of absence create the exposure. A vacant inherited house, a rental left empty after a tenant moved out, or a lot nobody has walked in years are the situations where a claim could grow over time.

What a claimant has to prove

Maryland courts apply three elements: possession that is actual, open, notorious and exclusive; possession that is continuous for the full period; and possession that is hostile and under a claim of title or ownership. Appellate opinions quote this three-part test from Senez v. Collins.

The claimant carries the burden of showing the elements for 20 years. Under Hungerford v. Hungerford, every element must be shown, and if one is missing the possession doesn't give title.

  • Actual, open, notorious, exclusive: Living in or openly using the house in a way the owner could see, without sharing control with the owner
  • Continuous for 20 years: No long gaps in use during the period
  • Hostile, under claim of title: Occupying as if the owner, not with the owner's permission

Permission matters. Someone who stays with the owner's consent, or under a lease, isn't hostile in the legal sense. A written record of who was allowed in can help you later.

Removing someone from your property

The route depends on who the person is. A current or former tenant goes through the landlord-tenant process. Someone with no lease and no right to be there can be removed through a wrongful detainer case or, since October 2025, a sheriff affidavit for fraudulent occupancy.

For tenants and holdovers, the landlord first wins a judgment in a rent court, breach of lease or holding over case, then petitions for a warrant of restitution. A sheriff or constable must be present at the eviction, and it can't happen on a Sunday or a holiday. Owners can't lock out an occupant on their own.

For an unauthorized occupant who is not a tenant, the wrongful detainer action in Real Property 14-132 applies. It is a District Court case for someone holding possession without the right to it. It can't be used against a current tenant, a holdover tenant or someone with a court order protecting their possession.

  • Lease or rent history exists: use the landlord-tenant case and a warrant of restitution.
  • No lease and no permission: consider wrongful detainer.
  • Unsure of the occupant's status: ask a Maryland attorney before acting.

2025 changes for squatters

Senate Bill 46 (Chapter 188 of the 2025 laws) took effect October 1, 2025. It created a new crime of fraudulent occupancy and sped up the wrongful detainer process.

Under the new Criminal Law 8-906, it is a misdemeanor to occupy or claim a right to occupy a residence you have no lawful right to, with intent to defraud. A first violation carries up to 90 days in jail, a fine up to $500, or both. A second violation within two years rises to up to six months and $1,000, and later violations within two years of the previous one go up to one year and $2,500.

An owner can file a sworn affidavit with the county sheriff saying a person is fraudulently in possession. The sheriff must then remove that person and return the property, but a deputy may not remove an occupant who shows evidence of lawful possession. The offense doesn't apply where a court order granted possession or where a remedy exists under Title 8 of the Real Property Article, so landlord-tenant disputes stay in court.

Wrongful detainer deadlines

The process is faster than it used to be. The same 2025 act set tight deadlines for each step.

StepRule in Chapter 188
SummonsMay be addressed to OCCUPANT LOCATED AT the property address when the name is unknown
HearingNo more than 10 business days after the complaint is filed
ServiceCompleted within 4 business days; after two good-faith attempts on different days, mailing plus posting counts
DefaultCourt must enter a default judgment if the defendant does not attend
AppealDeadline cut from 10 days to 4 days after judgment

The owner still has to show a legal interest in the property. If the court finds the owner entitled to possession, it issues a warrant directing the sheriff to deliver possession immediately. Damages and fees may be awarded if they were claimed in the complaint. Older guides online may mention a 10 day appeal period, which no longer applies.

How an adverse possession claim affects a sale

A claim, or even a rumor of one, clouds title and can stall a closing. Buyers and their title companies will ask who occupies the property and on what basis.

Real Property 14-108 lets a person in peaceable possession, under color of title or claim of right, bring a quiet title action in the circuit court where the land sits. The adverse claim does not have to be actively asserted. A suit of this kind must name anyone who appears of record or who claims a hostile outstanding right. An old boundary dispute or an occupant's claim of ownership can end up before a judge before a clean sale is possible.

Cash Home Buyers works with Maryland sellers who have occupied, inherited or neglected houses, and we buy as-is. If someone is living in a house you own, first find out whether they are a tenant, a guest or an unauthorized occupant, because that decides which court process applies.

  • Keep copies of leases, texts and receipts that show whether the occupant had permission.
  • Photograph the property and record the dates you last inspected it.
  • Pay taxes and keep insurance active on a vacant house.
  • Do not change locks or remove belongings before a court order.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maryland houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Protecting a vacant house

Visit the property regularly, keep records of those visits and act quickly when someone is in the house without permission.

The legislature is still working on the topic. Senate Bill 989 from 2025 proposed a sheriff registry of unauthorized occupants for owners of residential dwellings, with enrollment for six months. Bring your visit log, photographs and any lease or permission records to the first meeting with an attorney or the sheriff's office, since those papers show how long the house was empty and who had a right to be inside. If the house is more trouble than it is worth, selling it as-is for cash ends the exposure.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Maryland?

The statute sets 20 years from when the owner's cause of action accrues. Courts also require the possession to be continuous and hostile for that full period.

Is a squatter the same as a tenant in Maryland?

No. A tenant has a lease or rental agreement, and the owner removes a tenant through the landlord-tenant court process and a warrant of restitution. An unauthorized occupant with no lease can be the subject of a wrongful detainer case.

Can the sheriff remove a squatter in Maryland?

Yes in some cases. Since October 1, 2025, an owner can file a sworn affidavit of fraudulent occupancy with the county sheriff, but the sheriff may not remove someone who shows evidence of lawful possession.

How fast is wrongful detainer in Maryland?

The hearing must be no more than 10 business days after the complaint is filed, and service must be completed within 4 business days. The appeal deadline is now 4 days.

Can I change the locks on someone living in my house?

No. For tenants, eviction needs a court judgment and a warrant of restitution carried out with the sheriff or constable present.

content:
Maryland Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Lease requirements

Maryland sets a few mandatory lease items, and some clauses can't be enforced at all. Under Real Property § 8-208, a landlord offering five or more dwelling units must use a written lease. Without one, the tenancy is presumed to run for one year from first occupancy unless the tenant ends it with one month's written notice.

Every lease must include:

  • A statement about the habitability of the premises, or the condition the parties agreed on
  • Each party's duties for heat, gas, electricity, water and repairs
  • A receipt for the security deposit
  • A copy of the current Maryland Tenants' Bill of Rights from the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs in the Department of Housing and Community Development

A landlord must also hand a prospective applicant the proposed lease on written request, with no signature or deposit required.

Lease clauses a landlord can't enforce

Section 8-208 lists terms that are unenforceable. A tenant can recover actual damages and attorney's fees if a landlord includes or tries to use one. Prohibited terms include:

  • Confession of judgment, or a waiver of the tenant's legal remedies or a jury trial
  • A shorter notice-to-quit period than the law requires
  • A right to take the premises or the tenant's belongings without termination and formal legal process, unless the property is abandoned
  • A penalty on a tenant for calling law enforcement or emergency services
  • A waiver of the tenant's right of first refusal under § 8-119

Late fees are capped at 5% of the rent due for the period. On weekly leases the cap is $3 per week or $12 per month. An automatic renewal clause longer than a month must be set apart with room for the tenant's written acknowledgment, or the landlord can't enforce it.

Security deposit rules

The landlord must give a receipt, keep the money in a proper account, and offer a move-out inspection. The receipt has to tell the tenant about the right to a move-in inspection and the right to be present at the move-out inspection. It also has to warn that noncompliance can mean a penalty of up to three times the deposit withheld plus attorney's fees. Without a receipt the landlord owes the tenant $25, and copies must be kept for two years.

Deposit ruleMaryland requirement
Where it is heldInsured institutions with in-state branches, in interest-bearing accounts used only for deposits
When it is depositedWithin 30 days of receipt
Tenant's request to attend inspectionCertified mail at least 15 days before moving, with move date and new address
Timing of inspectionWithin five days before or after the move date
InterestSimple interest, no less than 1.5% a year, only on deposits of $50 or more, and none unless held six months

A landlord who skips the inspection steps forfeits the right to withhold money for damages.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maryland house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens to the deposit when a landlord sells

The seller stays liable for the deposit unless the full amount and an accounting go to the buyer. Under § 8-203, the original landlord remains responsible for the deposit plus interest until it is transferred with an accounting to the transferee. Any successor in interest is liable for failing to return it.

A new landlord must accept a tenant's surety bond and can't demand an extra deposit during the current term. Creditors of either party can't attach the deposit.

If you're planning a sale, reconcile the deposit records before closing. That transfer and accounting is what moves the liability off you. In a cash sale with a short timeline, pull the ledger and the tenant's receipt early so the numbers are ready when the buyer's side asks for them.

Do tenants get a right of first refusal when the owner sells?

In many cases, yes. Section 8-119 gives tenants of one to three unit residential rentals a right of first refusal. The tenant must have lived there six months or more and be named on the written lease.

  • Owner plans a public listing: Send notice before listing. The tenant has 30 days to make a written offer, and the owner has five days to accept or counter.
  • Owner gets an unsolicited third-party offer: Send notice at that price. The tenant has 30 days to match before the owner can accept.
  • Third-party offer at least 10% below the lowest price offered to the tenant: Notice and a new 30 day window
  • Tenant declines early: Owner may list

Many transfers are exempt, including sales to family members, foreclosure and tax sales, estate and trust administration, transfers by will or inheritance, and properties of four or more units. A violation carries a fine of up to $1,000, and liability stays with the owner rather than the property after closing. Owners send copies of notices to the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs through its website.

Rent increase notice

For a lease term longer than a month, the landlord must give at least 90 days written notice before a rent increase. Section 8-209 sets shorter periods for shorter terms: 60 days for a term over one week up to one month, and 7 days for a week or less under a written lease (21 days if there is no written lease).

Notice goes by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, or electronically if the tenant elected that. A landlord can't make electronic notice a condition of the lease application. Local laws may require longer notice. Whoever holds the landlord's position when the increase is sent is bound by these rules, so a new owner who plans to raise rent after closing should count the days from the date notice actually goes out.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maryland houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Eviction for unpaid rent

It begins with a written notice and a 10 day cure period, then a District Court case. Under § 8-401, the notice must state the intent to sue for possession, and the complaint must give the date the notice was delivered.

  • Trial is set for the fifth day after filing.
  • If the court finds rent due, possession is ordered within 4 days after trial. A physician's certificate can extend that up to 15 days.
  • A warrant of restitution can issue after 7 days. The landlord must order it within 60 days of the judgment or the possession judgment is stricken.
  • Warrants are stayed during extreme weather and must be executed within 5 days after conditions end.
  • Either side may appeal to circuit court within 4 days.

A tenant can redeem by paying all past-due amounts, court costs and fees before the eviction is carried out, unless the tenant has three rent-related possession judgments in the prior 12 months.

Eviction for breaking another lease term

For a lease with a stated term that allows repossession on breach, § 8-402.1 requires 30 days written notice, or 14 days where the behavior shows clear and imminent danger of serious harm. The landlord then files a written complaint in District Court.

The court must find the breach substantial before it orders eviction. Either party may appeal to circuit court within 10 days. Accepting a payment after the notice doesn't waive the breach notice or the possession judgment unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.

Rent escrow and retaliation

A tenant can use rent escrow only for serious, dangerous defects such as no heat, light or running water, inadequate sewage disposal, or serious structural or fire hazards. Under § 8-211, cosmetic problems, small cracks and a lack of air conditioning are presumed not to qualify, and the tenant must first notify the landlord. A wait of more than 30 days after notice is presumed unreasonable.

Section 8-208.1 bars retaliation for good-faith complaints, joining a lawsuit, taking part in a tenants' organization, or calling police or emergency services. A tenant who wins can recover damages up to three months' rent plus fees. An action taken more than six months after a protected act isn't treated as retaliatory.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does a Maryland landlord have to use a written lease?

Yes if the landlord offers five or more dwelling units. Without a written lease the tenancy is presumed to last one year from first occupancy.

How much can a Maryland landlord charge as a late fee?

No more than 5% of the rent due for the period. For weekly installments the limit is $3 a week or $12 a month.

What notice is needed for a rent increase?

For a term longer than one month, at least 90 days written notice. Shorter terms have 60 or 7 day notice periods, and local laws can add more.

Do tenants get first chance to buy a rental house in Maryland?

Often. One to three unit rentals fall under the right of first refusal in § 8-119 for tenants who have lived there six months and are on the lease, with a 30 day window and many exemptions.

Who is liable for the security deposit after a sale?

The original landlord stays liable unless the full deposit and an accounting are transferred to the new owner. Any successor in interest is also liable for failing to return it.

title: Maryland Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Maryland Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Maryland
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Maryland Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Maryland Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Maryland Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Maryland House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Maryland?
We buy Maryland houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Written notices a Maryland landlord must give

There are four main ones, and each runs on its own clock: a notice of intent to sue for unpaid rent, a breach notice, a notice that ends the tenancy, and a final notice of the eviction date. The reason for the eviction picks the notice. A defective one can lead a court to dismiss the complaint or vacate a warrant.

SituationNotice and length
Unpaid rent (Real Property § 8-401)Written notice of intent to file, 10 days to pay
Lease violation, fixed-term lease (§ 8-402.1)30 days written notice
Violation showing clear and imminent danger (§ 8-402.1)14 days written notice
Ending a month-to-month tenancy or a written lease term over one week (§ 8-402)60 days
Ending a year-to-year tenancy (§ 8-402)90 days (180 for farm tenancies other than tobacco)
Ending a week-to-week tenancy (§ 8-402)7 days with a written lease, 21 days without
Warrant of restitution issued (§ 8-407)At least 6 days before the scheduled eviction

The 10-day nonpayment notice

The notice must be on the Judiciary's form, DC-CV-115, and it gives the tenant 10 days to pay before the landlord may file. Section 8-401 allows delivery by certified first-class mail, by posting on the door, or electronically if the tenant chose that method. Electronic notice needs proof of transmission.

The landlord's sworn complaint must state the date the notice was given, and the court may dismiss a complaint for sufficient cause. Only base rent counts toward the 10-day demand. Utilities, maintenance and other charges do not. Late fees are capped too: no more than 5 percent of the late rent, and on a partial payment the fee can apply only to the unpaid portion.

What changes for a lease violation?

The landlord has to wait 30 days after giving written notice that the tenant is in violation and that the landlord wants the property back. Section 8-402.1 covers a fixed-term lease that allows repossession for a breach, and the tenant or person in possession must refuse to comply.

If the breach shows a clear and imminent danger of serious harm to people or property, the wait is cut to 14 days. A tenant ordered out can still appeal to the circuit court within 10 days of the judgment and remain in the home by filing an affidavit, posting a bond, paying back rent and court costs, and covering the landlord's losses from the holdover.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Maryland house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Ending a tenancy without a violation

For most residential tenancies, the landlord gives 60 days. Real Property § 8-402(c) sets 60 days for a month-to-month tenancy or a written lease for a stated term over one week, 90 days for year-to-year, and 7 or 21 days for week-to-week depending on whether there is a written lease.

A few related rules shape the timeline:

  • If the landlord has received a notice of intent to foreclose and wants to end the tenancy, the notice is at least 30 days for month-to-month or week-to-week tenancies and 60 days for year-to-year. The rule does not reach Baltimore City or Montgomery County, landlords with five or more residential units in the state, or a property under a docketing order.
  • Taking rent after notice does not waive the notice or a judgment unless the parties agree otherwise in writing.
  • A tenant who stays past the end of the lease owes at least prorated rent at the lease rate for the holdover period.
  • A rent increase generally takes effect only at renewal and needs 90 days written notice, unless it is part of a notice ending the tenancy.

The final 6-day eviction notice

This notice goes out three ways at once and must carry specific details. Section 8-407 calls for first-class mail with a certificate of mailing, a posting on the front door backed by a date-stamped photo, and email or text if the landlord has the tenant's address or number.

The notice has to include:

  • The court case number, the tenant's name as used in the case and the property address
  • The date the warrant was ordered and the initial eviction date
  • A statement that the eviction can be avoided by returning possession or, where available, by redeeming, with the amount due if redemption is still open
  • A statement that this is the final notice even if the eviction is delayed
  • A warning that belongings may be lost, a list of legal help resources, and the landlord's phone, email and mailing address

A landlord may charge the tenant no more than $5 for giving it. If the landlord hands the sheriff or constable the mailing certificate, a timestamped door photo and a signed affidavit from whoever posted the notice, notice is presumed proper, though a tenant can challenge that. When the sheriff doubts notice was given, the warrant cannot be carried out without a further court order. Local governments may set the notice period anywhere from 4 to 14 days.

Actions a landlord cannot take

Lockouts and utility shutoffs are both banned. Under § 8-216, a landlord can take possession only through a warrant of restitution carried out by a sheriff or constable, or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

Section 8-208.1 also bars suing for possession, or ending a periodic tenancy, because a tenant made a good-faith complaint, joined a tenants' group, took part in a lawsuit against the landlord, or called police or emergency services. The tenant can raise this as a defense or as a damages claim, with damages up to three months' rent plus fees. Retaliation relief generally requires the tenant to be current on rent, and anything done more than six months after the protected activity cannot be treated as retaliatory. The section has no exception for a landlord who is selling.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Maryland houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When the landlord wants to sell a rented house

For a rental with three or fewer dwelling units, the owner generally must offer the tenant a chance to buy before listing or marketing the home. Real Property § 8-119 gives that right to a named lessee who has lived in the property at least six months.

The owner mails written notice on the form set by the Secretary of Housing and Community Development, by first-class mail with a certificate of mailing or by a tracked delivery service, and sends a copy to the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs. The tenant then has 30 days to deliver a written offer. If the offer matches the notice terms, the owner has 5 days to accept. A violation can bring a fine of up to $1,000.

The section does not cover several kinds of transfers, including:

  • Sales to a family member or to a business the owner wholly owns
  • Transfers by foreclosure, tax sale, court order or bankruptcy
  • Transfers by an estate, guardianship or trust fiduciary, or by will or inheritance

A landlord may enter to show the home to buyers on 24 hours written notice, generally Monday through Saturday between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Properties with four or more units fall outside the right of first refusal.

Frequently asked questions

How many days notice before a landlord files for unpaid rent?

Ten days. The landlord uses the Judiciary's form DC-CV-115, states the rent due, and gives the tenant 10 days to pay before filing in District Court.

How long is a notice to end a month-to-month tenancy?

Sixty days in writing from the landlord. The tenant generally gives 30 days, unless the lease requires more.

Can a landlord evict on 14 days notice?

Only for a lease violation that shows a clear and imminent danger of serious harm to people or property. Other breach notices run 30 days.

Is notice required before the sheriff arrives?

Yes. After a warrant of restitution, the landlord must send written notice at least 6 days before the scheduled eviction by mail, posting and electronic message when contact details are known. Some local governments set 4 to 14 days.

Does a tenant get first chance to buy a rented house?

Often. A named tenant of at least six months in a property with three or fewer units has a right of first refusal, with exceptions for family transfers, foreclosure, estate transfers and a few others.
